The story behind an idea

Mesmer, Franklin and one of the first blind trials

In 1784 a commission including Benjamin Franklin and Lavoisier tested "animal magnetism" by blindfolding patients.

Franz Anton Mesmer (1734–1815) held that an invisible fluid, "animal magnetism", flowed through bodies and that blockages in it caused illness. In Paris his sessions were a sensation: patients sat around a tub fitted with iron rods, and many went into convulsive "crises" before feeling better.

The royal commission

In 1784, Louis XVI commissioned a study from a panel that included Benjamin Franklin, the chemist Antoine Lavoisier and the physician Joseph-Ignace Guillotin. They did something new: they blindfolded people and led them to believe they were being magnetised when they were not, and vice versa. Reactions appeared when people believed it was being applied, not when it actually was.

They concluded that the effects were due to imagination. It is one of the first examples of a blinded trial, and of the power of expectation that we now call the placebo effect. Decades later, mesmerism led to the study of hypnosis.

References

  1. Franklin, B. et al. (1784/2002). Report of the commissioners charged by the King with the examination of animal magnetism. International Journal of Clinical and Experimental Hypnosis, 50(4), 332–363.
  2. Herr, H. W. (2005). Franklin, Lavoisier, and Mesmer: origin of the controlled clinical trial. Urologic Oncology, 23(5), 346–351.
